title: RGDM: Robust Graph Diffusion Model

paper.title: RGDM: Robust Graph Diffusion Model
paper.abstract:
Abstract Diffusion models represent a powerful class of generative models known for their solid theoretical foundations and remarkable performance across diverse tasks and domains. Existing node level diffusion methods synthesize nodes and edges within a graph, but are not designed to learn a robust generator from adversarially corrupted graphs. In this study, we introduce the Robust Graph Diffusion Model (RGDM), designed to generate labeled synthetic graph structures consisting of nodes and edges that integrate seamlessly into a given graph.
The RGDM consists of a Robust Graph Autoencoder (RGAE) and a Latent Diffusion Model (LDM). Leveraging an edge selection mechanism and an innovative low-rank regularization on the latent feature, the RGDM produces clean and high-quality synthetic graph structures, even when trained on graphs subject to adversarial attacks. Comprehensive experimental evaluations reveal that Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) trained on the augmented graph, which is formed by merging the original attacked graph with the synthetic graph structures, exhibit significantly improved robustness against various graph adversarial attacks in the context of semi-supervised node classification.
The code of the RGDM is available at https://github.com/Statistical-Deep-Learning/RGDM .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Building on the success of diffusion and latent diffusion models, recent works use diffusion-generated data to augment training sets ( Trabucco et al., 2024 ; Azizi et al., 2023 ) . However, extensions to graphs ( Niu et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Haefeli et al., 2022 ; Vignac et al., 2023 ; Limnios et al., 2023 ) mainly target graph-level augmentation. Most node-level methods expand labels through mix-up ( Han et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2021 ; Verma et al., 2021 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ; Jeong et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2024 ) or GAN-based synthesis for imbalance ( Jia et al., 2023a ; Wu et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2018 ; Liang et al., 2020 ; Yang et al., 2019 ) . Node level diffusion methods DoG ( Wang et al., 2025 ) and LR-FGDM ( Wang et al., 2026 ) share the autoencoder and diffusion template, but do not train the generator specifically for adversarial robustness. Moreover, GANs can be unstable and produce distributions misaligned with real data ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) . As a result, the challenge of generating synthetic graph structures (SGS) within a given graph, which are the synthetic nodes and their corresponding edges, in a robust manner to enhance node classification under attacks, remains underexplored. In this work, we tackle the problem of node-level graph generation and propose the Robust Graph Diffusion Model (RGDM), designed to synthesize high-quality graph structures within a single graph, even under adversarial attacks. These synthetic structures include both synthetic nodes and edges connecting them within the same graph, forming an augmented graph as illustrated in Figure 1 . Robust GNNs will be trained on the augmented graph, and superior performance is expected due to the enlarged set of labeled nodes. Generating high-quality SGS in adversarial scenarios for improved performance is challenging, important, and unaddressed in the robust graph learning literature. To address this challenge, RGDM integrates a Robust Graph Autoencoder (RGAE) with a Latent Diffusion Model (LDM). The RGAE incorporates an edge selection mechanism and a low-rank regularization on the latent features to counteract adversarial perturbations in the attacked graph. The low-rank regularization is motivated by the Low Frequency Property (LFP) ( Rahaman et al., 2019 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Cao et al., 2021 ; Choraria et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) : in the evaluated latent spaces, label information is more concentrated in leading eigendirections than adversarial perturbations (Section F.1 ). Theorem 3.1 provides a complementary, conditional justification through the spectral complexity of a bounded linear probe on this latent space. It is not a guarantee for the downstream GNN trained on the augmented graph. Figure 1 : Illustration of the 2-hop neighborhood of a real node and a synthetic node in the augmented graph. Figure 5 in Section F.10 illustrates the t-SNE visualization of the augmented graph. Figure 1 illustrates the 2-hop neighborhood of a real node and a synthetic node that have similar node features, evidenced by the t-SNE visualization in Figure 5 in Section F.10 of the appendix. The fidelity evaluations in Tables 13 and 14 compare synthetic structures with clean reference graphs through Frechet Node Distance (FND) and Frechet Edge Distance (FED). RGDM has lower distances than vanilla DDPM ( Ho et al., 2020 ) and the compared node augmentation methods. On Pubmed under 25 % 25\% Metattack, its FND/FED are 3.95 / 5.34 3.95/5.34 , compared with 3.79 / 5.15 3.79/5.15 for the clean reference. These are empirical fidelity measurements. Clean graphs are used for evaluation, not for training RGDM. The augmentation pipeline retains the original attacked adjacency. Edge selection acts inside the generator, reducing the reproduction of unreliable connections. The generated labeled structures supply additional supervision and relatively clean message passing paths. On Citeseer, adding 785 785 synthetic edges changes the normalized perturbation density from 25 % 25\% to approximately 20.6 % 20.6\% . This is a denominator effect, not removal of the original perturbations or a causal robustness guarantee (Section F.4 ). Difference from diffusion based purification. Diffusion models have also been used for data and graph purification ( He et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) . Purifying an observed graph and generating additional labeled nodes with incident edges are different tasks. Graph level purification methods do not directly provide the node level augmentation interface of RGDM. Conversely, vanilla node generation trained on a corrupted graph can reproduce its noise. RGDM trains its robust generator without paired clean graphs. Section F.13 compares GDDM and DiffSP preprocessing with RGDM augmentation using the same SG-GSR backbone, while Section F.12 separately evaluates a purification adaptation of RGDM. Contributions. First, RGDM learns a robust node level generator through edge selection, sparse hierarchical reconstruction, and low rank regularization of the latent features used by diffusion. Its Sparse Hierarchical Edge Decoder (SHED) evaluates selected clusters instead of globally scoring every candidate neighbor. Controlled comparisons with DoG and LR-FGDM, componentwise ablations, and wall clock measurements distinguish these contributions from the shared autoencoder and diffusion architecture. Second, RGDM augments existing classifiers without changing their architecture or objective. We evaluate its incremental benefit with each backbone fixed, including SG-GSR ( In et al., 2024 ) , and report paired variability. The gains over this strong backbone are modest in absolute magnitude, but consistent in the tested settings. Fidelity, heterophily, and adaptive attack evaluations support this empirical conclusion. The linear probe theorem motivates the latent regularizer and does not establish an end to end robustness guarantee.

sections.heading: 2 Related Works
sections.text: Data Augmentation for Graph Learning. To improve the performance of GNNs, node-level graph data augmentation methods have been studied to modify the structure ( Gasteiger et al., 2019 ; Zhao et al., 2021b ; Rong et al., 2020 ; Feng et al., 2022 ; Lai et al., 2024 ) , features ( You et al., 2020 ; Kong et al., 2022 ; Azad and Fang, 2024 ) , or node labels ( You et al., 2020 ; Kong et al., 2022 ; Azad and Fang, 2024 ) . Studies have demonstrated that increasing the number of labeled nodes based on Mix-up strategies ( Han et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2021 ; Verma et al., 2021 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ; Jeong et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2024 ) can greatly enhance the performance of the GNNs. Recent works address node and edge imbalance by generating synthetic nodes and edges ( Qu et al., 2021 ; Zhao et al., 2021a ; Hsu et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2023 ; Hsu et al., 2023 ) , but predominantly rely on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). However, the computer vision literature ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) has demonstrated that GANs often exhibit instability during training and that the distribution of synthetic data generated by GANs poorly matches the distribution of real data. Graph level diffusion models ( Song et al., 2021 ; Niu et al., 2020 ; Haefeli et al., 2022 ; Vignac et al., 2023 ; Limnios et al., 2023 ) generate entire graphs. DoG ( Wang et al., 2025 ) and LR-FGDM ( Wang et al., 2026 ) instead generate nodes and associated edges within an existing graph, as does RGDM. DoG reconstructs observed neighborhoods with a Bi-Level Neighborhood Decoder (BLND) and applies low rank regularization to its downstream GNN. LR-FGDM addresses few shot classification using a Hierarchical Graph Autoencoder (HGAE) with prototypical regularization, followed by a low rank transductive classifier. RGDM places edge selection, a sparsification objective, and low rank regularization inside the generator. Its TNN penalty acts on the latent features used by diffusion. SHED reconstructs selected sparse neighborhoods rather than all observed connections. The resulting augmented graph can be used with GCN, Pro-GNN, or SG-GSR. Tables 4 and 5 compare these methods with a fixed backbone. Table 35 additionally compares hierarchical reconstruction variants. Graph Adversarial Attacks and Defense. Despite the success of GNNs in graph-structured tasks ( Kipf and Welling, 2017 ; Zhang and Chen, 2018 ) , recent studies reveal their vulnerability to adversarial attacks ( Dai et al., 2022 ) . Depending on the attack objective, threat models are categorized as: targeted attacks ( Zügner et al., 2018 ) , which mislead predictions on specific nodes, and untargeted attacks ( Zügner and Günnemann, 2019 ; Sun et al., 2020 ) , which reduce overall model accuracy. To defend against these threats, robust learning strategies are grouped into three categories: adversarial training, graph processing, and model robustification. Adversarial training ( Li et al., 2022a ; Feng et al., 2019 ) augments training data with crafted adversarial samples. Graph processing ( Wu et al., 2019 ; Entezari et al., 2020 ; Jin et al., 2020 ; Lei et al., 2022 ) seeks to denoise perturbed graphs. Model robustification ( Xie et al., 2023 ; Rusch et al., 2022 ; Song et al., 2022 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ; Jia et al., 2023b ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Abbahaddou et al., 2024 ; In et al., 2024 ) enhances model resilience.

sections.heading: 3.4 Training GNNs on the Augmented Graph
sections.text: After obtaining the augmented graph 𝒢 aug {\cal G}_{\textup{aug}} , we then train either the vanilla GCN ( Kipf and Welling, 2017 ) or the robust GNNs, Pro-GNN ( Jin et al., 2020 ) and SG-GSR ( In et al., 2024 ) , on 𝒢 aug {\cal G}_{\textup{aug}} . sections.heading: 5 Conclusions
sections.text: We present the Robust Graph Diffusion Model (RGDM), marking the first robust graph diffusion model designed to generate synthetic graph structures, which are the synthetic nodes and synthetic edges connecting to them in the graph, for the node classification task. In addition, the RGDM significantly mitigates the negative effects of graph adversarial attacks and generates faithful synthetic graph structures, benefiting from the edge selection mechanism and the low-rank latent feature learning in the RGAE. The experiment results show that incorporating the synthetic graph structures into the original attacked graph for the training of GNNs significantly improves the classification accuracy for the semi-supervised node classification under various types of graph adversarial attacks.

sections.heading: Appendix B Further Explanation of Theorem 3.1
sections.text: Theorem 3.1 concerns the RGAE latent matrix 𝐙 \mathbf{Z} , which is the input to conditional diffusion, and an auxiliary bounded linear probe. Its two substantive terms are the empirical label fitting error and a complexity tradeoff between rank and spectral tail. The spectral tail is normalized by N N , in accordance with the spectrum of 𝐊 / N \mathbf{K}/N in [ 87 ] . The STLC specialization has neither a log ⁡ N \log N multiplier nor an N / u N/u prefactor, and it places no restriction on the relative split sizes beyond m , u ≥ 2 m,u\geq 2 . Its confidence term uses s = min ⁡ { m , u } s=\min\left\{m,u\right\} and the classwise union term log ⁡ C \log C . Reducing a spectral tail at fixed rank lowers that candidate complexity term if the feature scale and probe norm bounds are fixed. It does not ensure a reduction in the empirical fitting error, the scale constants, or the total bound after retraining the representation. In particular, the LFP does not by itself imply that labels are exactly representable in the retained subspace or that their training residual vanishes. Neither graph homophily nor spectral smoothness of labels with respect to the adjacency matrix is assumed. Strong heterophily may require additional latent directions: a smaller r r can then increase T r T_{r} or the fitting error. The soft coefficient τ T \tau_{\textup{T}} and cross validated starting rank balance this tradeoff, rather than enforcing one hard rank on every graph. The Chameleon and Actor experiments support the selected settings empirically. They do not guarantee that low rank regularization always improves heterophilic graphs. The probability statement conditions on a fixed representation independent of the fresh probe split. If representation learning or an attack uses those probe labels to select 𝐙 \mathbf{Z} , this theorem cannot simply be applied conditionally to that selected matrix. In the actual RGDM pipeline, the downstream classifier is trained on decoded node attributes and edges, not on 𝐙 \mathbf{Z} . The low rank ablation (Table 3 ) and FND/FED results (Tables 13 to 14 ) support this second, empirical link. Establishing a joint generalization and robustness theory for data dependent representation learning, class conditional generation, and the downstream GNN is future work. sections.heading: E.2 Training Settings
sections.text: The training of the RGAE is divided into two phases. In the first phase, we pre-train the RGAE by only optimizing the consistency loss ℒ C ( t ) {\cal L}^{(t)}_{\textup{C}} in Equation ( 1 ) for 2000 epochs. In the second phase, we optimize ℒ ( t ) {\cal L}^{(t)} for another 1000 epochs. We use the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001 0.001 for the training. The weight decay is set to 1 × 10 − 5 1\times 10^{-5} . We train the LDM in the RGDM after finishing the training of the RGAE. We use the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.0002 0.0002 to train the LDM for 3000 3000 epochs. To mitigate the effects of potentially unstable masks 𝐒 inter \mathbf{S}_{\textup{inter}} and 𝐒 intra \mathbf{S}_{\textup{intra}} during early training, we adopt a warm-up strategy widely used in graph structure learning. During the first 100 100 epochs, the RGAE is trained only with the reconstruction loss and the low-rank regularization term while keeping 𝐒 inter \mathbf{S}_{\textup{inter}} and 𝐒 intra \mathbf{S}_{\textup{intra}} fixed to the original hierarchical edge maps.

sections.heading: E.3 Attack Settings
sections.text: Non-targeted Adversarial Attacks (Metattack) [ 101 ] . We first evaluate the robustness of our method against the non-targeted adversarial attack method Metattack. Metattack treats the graph as a hyperparameter to optimize and uses the meta-gradients to solve the bi-level optimization problem, which minimizes the node classification accuracy. We follow the implementation in [ 101 ] . As Metattack has several variants, we follow [ 37 ] and adopt the most destructive attack version, Meta-Self, on Cora, Citeseer, and Polblogs datasets. On Pubmed, we adopt the approximate version of Meta-Self, A-Meta-Self, following the settings in [ 37 ] . We measure the strength of the attack by the perturbation rate, which is the ratio of perturbed edges among all the edges in the graph. We evaluate the RGDM and all the baselines with the perturbation rates ranging from 0 0 to 25 % 25\% with a step of 5 % 5\% . Targeted Adversarial Attack (Nettack) [ 100 ] . We adopt Nettack as the targeted attack method in evaluating the robustness of our method. Nettack manipulates the edges and node features to degrade the classification accuracy on the target nodes while minimizing the change in the graph’s degree distribution and the feature co-occurrences. We use the default attack settings in the original implementation in [ 100 ] . The nodes in the test set whose degree is larger than 10 10 are set as the target nodes. The number of perturbations made on every targeted node is defined as the attack budget. Following [ 37 ] , we evaluate the RGDM and all the baselines with attack budgets ranging from 1 1 to 5 5 with a step size of 1 1 . Following the settings in [ 37 ] , we only sample 10 % 10\% of the target nodes for the evaluation on the Nettack. Gradient-based Attack Method (Topology Attack) [ 82 ] . We evaluate the robustness of the RGDM against a gradient-based attack method named Topology Attack [ 82 ] . The topology Attack proposes a projected gradient descent (PGD) adversarial attack method that perturbs the edges in a graph to degrade the overall node classification accuracy on the perturbed graph. We adopt the same settings in [ 82 ] to attack the graphs in our experiments. Similar to the settings for Metattack, we measure the strength of the attack by the perturbation rate, which is the ratio of the perturbed edges among all the edges in the graph. We evaluate the RGDM and all the baselines with perturbation rates ranging from 0 0 to 25 % 25\% with a step of 5 % 5\% .

sections.heading: E.6 Compared Methods
sections.text: In our empirical evaluation, we comprehensively benchmark the proposed RGDM against various GNNs, including models that exemplify advances in expressive power, structural modeling, and resilience to adversarial or noisy perturbations. The standard GNN baselines include Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN) [ 38 ] , Graph Attention Networks (GAT) [ 68 ] , and Relational GCNs (RGCN) [ 98 ] , which serve as foundational architectures widely adopted for semi-supervised node classification. Additionally, we incorporate GCN-SVD [ 18 ] , which leverages truncated singular value decomposition to mitigate the impact of noisy graph spectra. To rigorously assess the robustness of RGDM under adversarial settings, we further compare it with the state-of-the-art robust GNNs explicitly designed to enhance stability and generalization in the presence of graph corruption. These include GraphBel [ 62 ] , which integrates belief propagation with GNNs for noise-tolerant inference; UAG [ 19 ] , which unifies adversarial training with graph structure learning; GCORNs [ 1 ] , a framework that co-regularizes neighborhood consistency and robustness objectives; GADC [ 47 ] , which employs adaptive denoising through graph diffusion mechanisms; and HANG [ 92 ] , a hierarchical adversarial defense method. We also include Pro-GNN [ 37 ] , which jointly optimizes graph structure and model parameters via low-rank and sparsity constraints, and STABLE [ 43 ] , which stabilizes message passing through spectral smoothing.

F.3 Quality Evaluation of the Augmented Graph
sections.text: This paper introduces a novel graph diffusion model named RGDM, which synthesizes the graph structures. The synthetic graph structures generated by the RGDM are subsequently combined with the original attacked graph to form an augmented graph. By incorporating an edge selection mechanism in the RGDM, we aim to improve the robustness of the GNNs trained on the augmented graphs against the graph adversarial attacks. In Section 4.1 , we have shown that both the vanilla GCN and the robust GNNs trained on the augmented graph achieve significantly better performance for semi-supervised node classification under graph adversarial attacks. In this section, we directly evaluate the data quality of the synthetic graph structures generated by the RGDM. In the visual domain, the Frechet Inception Distance (FID) is a widely used metric to evaluate the quality of the synthetic images generated by the generative models [ 9 , 28 ] . The FID score measures the similarity between the distribution of the generated images and the distribution of the real images. To compute the FID score, the pre-trained Inception v3 [ 65 ] is used to extract the features from both the real images and the generated images, which are then modeled as the multivariate Gaussian distributions. The FID score is then calculated using the Frechet Distance (FD) [ 9 ] between the two multivariate Gaussian distributions modeling the real and the generated images [ 17 ] . A lower FID score indicates that the generated images are more similar to the real images, suggesting better quality. Quality Evaluation of the Synthetic Nodes. Although the Inception model cannot be applied to the graph data, we can replace the Inception model in the computation of the FID score with the pre-trained GCN [ 38 ] for extracting node features to adapt the metric to evaluate the quality of synthetic nodes generated by the RGDM. To this end, we define the Frechet Node Distance (FND), which is the FD between the multivariate Gaussians modeling the node features extracted by pre-trained GCN. We randomly split the nodes in the original clean graph into two partitions of equal size, which are the base partition and the test partition. To mitigate the influence of the randomness, we compute the FND scores with 10 10 different random splits and report the mean and the standard deviation of the FND scores across different runs. The FND computed between the nodes in the test partition and the base partition of the original clean graph establishes the baseline of the expected FND score for high-quality nodes. By computing the FND score between the features of nodes in the synthetic graph structures generated by the RGDM and the features of nodes in the base partition of the original clean graph, we evaluate the quality of the synthetic nodes in the synthetic graph structures. For simplicity, we refer to the FND score for the synthetic nodes as the FND between their features and the features of the nodes in the base partition of the original clean graph. To show the effectiveness of the robustness loss in the training of the RGAE for the RGDM, we also compute the FND for the nodes in the synthetic graph structures generated by the RGDM without the node robustness loss and the edge robustness loss. To demonstrate the advantages of the RGDM over the vanilla diffusion model, the DDPM [ 28 ] , we train a baseline DDPM model on the input node attributes of the original attacked graph and synthesize the same number of synthetic nodes as the RGDM. The synthetic edges are then generated by connecting each synthetic node to its K-nearest neighbors in the original attacked graph using the K-nearest neighbors (KNN) algorithm with K = ⌈ d ave ⌉ K=\lceil d_{\textup{ave}}\rceil , where d ave d_{\textup{ave}} is the average degree of the original clean graph. The synthetic graph structures, including the synthetic nodes and edges generated by the baseline DDPM model, are combined with the original attacked graph to form the augmented graph. Next, we compute the FND score for the nodes in the synthetic graph structures generated by the baseline DDPM model. In addition, we compute FND for nodes generated by the four baseline node augmentation methods, which are the iGraphMix [ 34 ] , ImGAGN [ 55 ] , Graphsmote [ 93 ] , and SNS [ 22 ] . We also calculate the FND score for nodes in the original attacked graph. We use the same GCN [ 38 ] pre-trained on the original clean graph to extract the node features for computing the FND score. sections.heading: F.6 Cross-validation on the Number of Synthetic Nodes
sections.text: In our experiments, we generate 10 × | 𝒱 L | 10\times\left|{\cal V}_{L}\right| synthetic nodes, where 𝒱 L {\cal V}_{L} is the training set of the original graph. Then, we search for the optimal size of synthetic nodes N ′ N^{\prime} added in the augmented graph from 1 × | 𝒱 L | 1\times\left|{\cal V}_{L}\right| to 10 × | 𝒱 L | 10\times\left|{\cal V}_{L}\right| with a step size of | 𝒱 L | \left|{\cal V}_{L}\right| . In the cross-validation, we train different GNN classifiers with different numbers of synthetic data and set N ′ N^{\prime} to the one that achieves the best validation accuracy by the end of 40 % 40\% of their total epoch number. To study the effectiveness of the cross-validation process for selecting the optimal number of synthetic nodes, we calculate the complete cross-validation time of different models on different datasets. All the experiments are performed on one Nvidia A100 GPU. It is observed from the results in Table 17 that the cross-validation process does not largely increase the computation overhead. sections.heading: F.7 Adversarial Defense on Large Scale Graphs
sections.text: To evaluate the scalability of the proposed method, we conduct additional experiments on graph adversarial defense for large-scale graph datasets, which are the large-scale social network, Reddit [ 25 ] , and the large-scale knowledge graph, ogbn-arxiv [ 32 ] . The statistics of the Reddit and ogbn-arxiv datasets are detailed in Table 9 . Since the Metattack [ 101 ] , the Nettack [ 100 ] , and the Topology Attack [ 82 ] adopted in Section 4.1 do not scale to large graphs at the size of Reddit and ogbn-arxiv, we use a scalable graph adversarial attack method, the improved DICE [ 44 ] , in our experiments on Reddit and ogbn-arxiv. The experiments are performed for perturbation rates of 0 % 0\% , 10 % 10\% , and 20 % 20\% following the settings in [ 44 ] with GCN as the baseline model. The results are shown in Table 21 . It is observed that RGDM consistently improves the performance of the GCN baseline across all perturbation levels on both datasets. For example, RGDM achieves an improvement of 2.25 % 2.25\% on ogbn-arxiv at the perturbation rate of 10 % 10\% , indicating its effectiveness in defending against adversarial perturbations even on large and complex knowledge graphs. sections.heading: F.8 Sensitivity Analysis on the Hyper-Parameters
sections.text: In this section, we conduct sensitivity analyses on the key hyper-parameters of RGDM, including the temperature parameter τ \tau for edge selection and the number of clusters K K in SHED. The study is carried out using RGDM (Pro-GNN) on the Cora dataset under a 25 % 25\% Metattack setting. As shown in Table 23 , although the highest accuracy is achieved at τ = 0.5 \tau=0.5 , the performance remains stable across different values of τ \tau . In particular, even the lowest performing setting, τ = 0.1 \tau=0.1 , results in only a marginal 0.19 % 0.19\% decrease in accuracy compared to the best result. Since SHED partitions the graph into K K balanced clusters and sets the maximum cluster size as M = ⌈ N / K ⌉ M=\lceil N/K\rceil , changing K K affects both the granularity of hierarchical edge decoding and the generation efficiency. As shown in Table 24 , RGDM is not sensitive to the choice of K K . The best performance is achieved at K = 100 K=100 , which is the default setting used in our experiments. sections.heading: F.12 Study on RGDM for Graph Purification
sections.text: The RGDM proposed in Section 3 has demonstrated superior performance for generative data augmentation (GDA), which involves generating faithful synthetic graph structures and integrating them into the original attacked graph to obtain an augmented graph. In this section, we study the effectiveness of applying RGDM to purify the attacked graph. The graph purification by RGDM, referred to as RGDM (Purification), is achieved by reconstructing each node and its corresponding edges through the LDM, where Gaussian noise derived from the original node and its edges is progressively denoised by the LDM and subsequently decoded by the GAE to produce clean node features and edges. The RGDM (Purification) variant only purifies the original graph, aiming to explore whether RGDM can be adapted to directly denoise/remove the adversarial perturbations in the original attacked graph. Moreover, the RGDM (Purification) can be combined with RGDM for GDA, denoted as RGDM (GDA) here, leading to a variant that performs both GDA and graph purification, denoted as RGDM (GDA + Purification). The study is performed on Cora under Metattack with a 25 % 25\% attack rate. Table 30 shows that applying RGDM for purification enhances the performance of Pro-GNN, while GDA with RGDM achieves better performance. Moreover, it is observed that combining GDA and graph purification by RGDM further improves the performance. Table 30 : Study on the effectiveness of graph purification and GDA by RGDM. The evaluation is conducted on Cora under Metattack with 25 % 25\% perturbation rate. Method Accuracy ( % \% ) Pro-GNN 69.7 RGDM (Purification) 71.0 RGDM (GDA) 72.3 RGDM (GDA + Purification) 72.9

sections.heading: F.16 Study on the Impact of Label Ratio
sections.text: To assess the robustness of RGDM (Pro-GNN) under varying levels of supervision, we evaluate performance on the Cora dataset under a 25 % 25\% Metattack perturbation rate while varying the labeled training ratio. In this study, we consider both sparse label regimes ( 2.5 % 2.5\% to 10 % 10\% ) and denser settings ( 20 % 20\% to 60 % 60\% ), with 10% of nodes fixed for validation and the remainder used for testing. As shown in Table 34 , RGDM consistently outperforms the Pro-GNN baseline across all label ratios. These results confirm that the improvements of RGDM are not confined to a specific supervision regime and generalize well across both low- and high-label density settings. sections.heading: F.18 Adaptive Attack Evaluation
sections.text: The experiments in Section 4.1 follow the commonly used attack-first-then-defend protocol, where the graph is first perturbed by adversarial attacks and the defense is then applied to the attacked graph. Although this protocol is widely adopted in graph adversarial robustness, it may not fully reflect a defense-aware adversary. In particular, an adaptive adversary may be aware of the RGDM pipeline and attack the augmented graph after the synthetic graph structures have been generated. To address this concern, we further evaluate RGDM under an adaptive attack setting, following the adaptive evaluation protocol in prior graph robustness studies [ 51 ] . Settings. We consider an adaptive version of Metattack [ 101 ] with a perturbation rate of 25 % 25\% . Different from the standard Metattack evaluation in Section 4.1 , where the attack is performed before RGDM augmentation, the adaptive attacker perturbs the final augmented graph 𝒢 aug {\cal G}_{\textup{aug}} used for training the downstream GNN. The attacker is aware of the full RGDM pipeline, including the generation of synthetic graph structures, edge selection, low-rank regularization, and the downstream SG-GSR classifier. For a fair comparison, the perturbation budget is fixed to the same number of edge perturbations as the 25 % 25\% Metattack on the original graph. We repeat each experiment 10 10 times with different random seeds and report the mean and standard deviation of node classification accuracy. Let n aug ≔ N + N ′ n_{\textup{aug}}\coloneqq N+N^{\prime} and let 𝐏 ∈ { 0 , 1 } n aug × n aug \mathbf{P}\in\left\{0,1\right\}^{n_{\textup{aug}}\times n_{\textup{aug}}} be a symmetric zero diagonal flip matrix. The defense aware attack searches over the admissible set in Equation ( 12 ): 𝒫 b ≔ { 𝐏 : 𝐏 = 𝐏 ⊤ , 𝐏 i ​ i = 0 , ∑ 1 ≤ i < j ≤ n aug 𝐏 i ​ j ≤ b } , 𝐀 aug adv ≔ 𝐀 aug ⊕ 𝐏 . \displaystyle{\cal P}_{b}\coloneqq\left\{\mathbf{P}:\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{P}^{\top},\ \mathbf{P}_{ii}=0,\ \sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n_{\textup{aug}}}\mathbf{P}_{ij}\leq b\right\},\qquad\mathbf{A}^{\textup{adv}}_{\textup{aug}}\coloneqq\mathbf{A}_{\textup{aug}}\oplus\mathbf{P}. (12) Here ⊕ \oplus denotes entrywise binary edge flipping. In Equation ( 12 ), b b is the same absolute number of flips used by the 25 % 25\% attack on the corresponding original graph, not 25 % 25\% of the larger augmented edge count. Candidate flips may involve original or synthetic nodes. The attacker knows the RGAE, edge selection mechanism, latent regularizer, LDM, and downstream classifier, and optimizes the Metattack surrogate against downstream retraining on the perturbed augmented graph. The first variant attacks the realized augmented graph. The second additionally differentiates its meta gradient through the relaxed edge selection mask: the forward pass thresholds 𝐒 ^ i ​ j = σ ⁡ ( 𝜽 i ​ j / τ ) \widehat{\mathbf{S}}_{ij}=\sigma(\bm{\theta}_{ij}/\tau) at 1 / 2 1/2 , and the backward pass uses its straight through gradient with τ = 0.5 \tau=0.5 . This is a gradient approximation to the discrete selection operation, not a proof of globally optimal adversarial perturbations. Knowledge of the LDM does not by itself establish differentiation through its entire stochastic sampling trajectory. The reported differentiable variant specifically tests the edge selection mechanism. Table 36: Adaptive attack evaluation under Metattack [ 101 ] with 25 % 25\% perturbation rate. Arizona State University Bellevue, WA 98004, USA Tempe, AZ 85281, USA pingli98@gmail.com {yancheng.wang,dsun30,yingzhen.yang}@asu.edu Abstract Diffusion models represent a powerful class of generative models known for their solid theoretical foundations and remarkable performance across diverse tasks and domains. Existing node level diffusion methods synthesize nodes and edges within a graph, but are not designed to learn a robust generator from adversarially corrupted graphs. In this study, we introduce the Robust Graph Diffusion Model (RGDM), designed to generate labeled synthetic graph structures consisting of nodes and edges that integrate seamlessly into a given graph. The RGDM consists of a Robust Graph Autoencoder (RGAE) and a Latent Diffusion Model (LDM). Leveraging an edge selection mechanism and an innovative low-rank regularization on the latent feature, the RGDM produces clean and high-quality synthetic graph structures, even when trained on graphs subject to adversarial attacks. Comprehensive experimental evaluations reveal that Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) trained on the augmented graph, which is formed by merging the original attacked graph with the synthetic graph structures, exhibit significantly improved robustness against various graph adversarial attacks in the context of semi-supervised node classification. The code of the RGDM is available at https://github.com/Statistical-Deep-Learning/RGDM . 1 Introduction Building on the success of diffusion and latent diffusion models, recent works use diffusion-generated data to augment training sets ( Trabucco et al., 2024 ; Azizi et al., 2023 ) . However, extensions to graphs ( Niu et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Haefeli et al., 2022 ; Vignac et al., 2023 ; Limnios et al., 2023 ) mainly target graph-level augmentation. Most node-level methods expand labels through mix-up ( Han et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2021 ; Verma et al., 2021 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ; Jeong et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2024 ) or GAN-based synthesis for imbalance ( Jia et al., 2023a ; Wu et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2018 ; Liang et al., 2020 ; Yang et al., 2019 ) . Node level diffusion methods DoG ( Wang et al., 2025 ) and LR-FGDM ( Wang et al., 2026 ) share the autoencoder and diffusion template, but do not train the generator specifically for adversarial robustness. Moreover, GANs can be unstable and produce distributions misaligned with real data ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) . As a result, the challenge of generating synthetic graph structures (SGS) within a given graph, which are the synthetic nodes and their corresponding edges, in a robust manner to enhance node classification under attacks, remains underexplored. In this work, we tackle the problem of node-level graph generation and propose the Robust Graph Diffusion Model (RGDM), designed to synthesize high-quality graph structures within a single graph, even under adversarial attacks. These synthetic structures include both synthetic nodes and edges connecting them within the same graph, forming an augmented graph as illustrated in Figure 1 . Robust GNNs will be trained on the augmented graph, and superior performance is expected due to the enlarged set of labeled nodes. Generating high-quality SGS in adversarial scenarios for improved performance is challenging, important, and unaddressed in the robust graph learning literature. To address this challenge, RGDM integrates a Robust Graph Autoencoder (RGAE) with a Latent Diffusion Model (LDM). The RGAE incorporates an edge selection mechanism and a low-rank regularization on the latent features to counteract adversarial perturbations in the attacked graph. The low-rank regularization is motivated by the Low Frequency Property (LFP) ( Rahaman et al., 2019 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Cao et al., 2021 ; Choraria et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) : in the evaluated latent spaces, label information is more concentrated in leading eigendirections than adversarial perturbations (Section F.1 ). Theorem 3.1 provides a complementary, conditional justification through the spectral complexity of a bounded linear probe on this latent space. It is not a guarantee for the downstream GNN trained on the augmented graph. Figure 1 : Illustration of the 2-hop neighborhood of a real node and a synthetic node in the augmented graph. Edge selection acts inside the generator, reducing the reproduction of unreliable connections. The generated labeled structures supply additional supervision and relatively clean message passing paths. This is a denominator effect, not removal of the original perturbations or a causal robustness guarantee (Section F.4 ). Difference from diffusion based purification. Diffusion models have also been used for data and graph purification ( He et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) . Purifying an observed graph and generating additional labeled nodes with incident edges are different tasks. Graph level purification methods do not directly provide the node level augmentation interface of RGDM. Conversely, vanilla node generation trained on a corrupted graph can reproduce its noise. RGDM trains its robust generator without paired clean graphs. Section F.13 compares GDDM and DiffSP preprocessing with RGDM augmentation using the same SG-GSR backbone, while Section F.12 separately evaluates a purification adaptation of RGDM. Contributions. First, RGDM learns a robust node level generator through edge selection, sparse hierarchical reconstruction, and low rank regularization of the latent features used by diffusion. Its Sparse Hierarchical Edge Decoder (SHED) evaluates selected clusters instead of globally scoring every candidate neighbor. Controlled comparisons with DoG and LR-FGDM, componentwise ablations, and wall clock measurements distinguish these contributions from the shared autoencoder and diffusion architecture. Second, RGDM augments existing classifiers without changing their architecture or objective. We evaluate its incremental benefit with each backbone fixed, including SG-GSR ( In et al., 2024 ) , and report paired variability. The gains over this strong backbone are modest in absolute magnitude, but consistent in the tested settings. Fidelity, heterophily, and adaptive attack evaluations support this empirical conclusion. The linear probe theorem motivates the latent regularizer and does not establish an end to end robustness guarantee. 2 Related Works Data Augmentation for Graph Learning. To improve the performance of GNNs, node-level graph data augmentation methods have been studied to modify the structure ( Gasteiger et al., 2019 ; Zhao et al., 2021b ; Rong et al., 2020 ; Feng et al., 2022 ; Lai et al., 2024 ) , features ( You et al., 2020 ; Kong et al., 2022 ; Azad and Fang, 2024 ) , or node labels ( You et al., 2020 ; Kong et al., 2022 ; Azad and Fang, 2024 ) . Studies have demonstrated that increasing the number of labeled nodes based on Mix-up strategies ( Han et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2021 ; Verma et al., 2021 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ; Jeong et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2024 ) can greatly enhance the performance of the GNNs. Recent works address node and edge imbalance by generating synthetic nodes and edges ( Qu et al., 2021 ; Zhao et al., 2021a ; Hsu et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2023 ; Hsu et al., 2023 ) , but predominantly rely on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). However, the computer vision literature ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) has demonstrated that GANs often exhibit instability during training and that the distribution of synthetic data generated by GANs poorly matches the distribution of real data. Graph level diffusion models ( Song et al., 2021 ; Niu et al., 2020 ; Haefeli et al., 2022 ; Vignac et al., 2023 ; Limnios et al., 2023 ) generate entire graphs. DoG ( Wang et al., 2025 ) and LR-FGDM ( Wang et al., 2026 ) instead generate nodes and associated edges within an existing graph, as does RGDM. DoG reconstructs observed neighborhoods with a Bi-Level Neighborhood Decoder (BLND) and applies low rank regularization to its downstream GNN. LR-FGDM addresses few shot classification using a Hierarchical Graph Autoencoder (HGAE) with prototypical regularization, followed by a low rank transductive classifier. RGDM places edge selection, a sparsification objective, and low rank regularization inside the generator. Its TNN penalty acts on the latent features used by diffusion. SHED reconstructs selected sparse neighborhoods rather than all observed connections. The resulting augmented graph can be used with GCN, Pro-GNN, or SG-GSR. Despite the success of GNNs in graph-structured tasks ( Kipf and Welling, 2017 ; Zhang and Chen, 2018 ) , recent studies reveal their vulnerability to adversarial attacks ( Dai et al., 2022 ) . Depending on the attack objective, threat models are categorized as: targeted attacks ( Zügner et al., 2018 ) , which mislead predictions on specific nodes, and untargeted attacks ( Zügner and Günnemann, 2019 ; Sun et al., 2020 ) , which reduce overall model accuracy. To defend against these threats, robust learning strategies are grouped into three categories: adversarial training, graph processing, and model robustification. Adversarial training ( Li et al., 2022a ; Feng et al., 2019 ) augments training data with crafted adversarial samples. Graph processing ( Wu et al., 2019 ; Entezari et al., 2020 ; Jin et al., 2020 ; Lei et al., 2022 ) seeks to denoise perturbed graphs. Model robustification ( Xie et al., 2023 ; Rusch et al., 2022 ; Song et al., 2022 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ; Jia et al., 2023b ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Abbahaddou et al., 2024 ; In et al., 2024 ) enhances model resilience. 3 Methods 3.1 Preliminaries of the Attributed Graph An attributed graph of N N nodes is represented by 𝒢 = ( 𝒱 , 𝐗 , 𝐀 ) {\cal G}=({\cal V},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{A}) , where 𝒱 = { v 1 , v 2 , … , v N } {\cal V}=\left\{v_{1},v_{2},\dots,v_{N}\right\} and ℰ ⊆ 𝒱 × 𝒱 {\cal E}\subseteq{\cal V}\times{\cal V} denote the nodes and edges respectively.
